revisions.title: A whispered request opens the inquiry
revisions.body: Lysis’s quiet request turns the scene toward Menexenus: he asks Socrates to repeat the same treatment with his friend, drawing the older man into a conversation not yet begun. Socrates accepts the assignment, then gives the request personal force by describing his own desire for a good friend as stronger than the usual hunger for horses, gold, or honors.

revisions.title: The opposite thesis turns against itself
revisions.body: The reported reversal begins from need: the poor needs the rich, the sick the doctor, and the ignorant the knower, so opposites seem to become friends through what one supplies the other. But Socrates turns that formula back on itself, asking whether it would make an enemy a friend and the good a friend of the bad. Those counterexamples put both simple likeness and opposition under pressure.

revisions.title: Desire changes the question
revisions.body: Once harmless desires remain in the thought experiment, bad can no longer explain every friendship. The conversation therefore shifts its causal question: desire is proposed as what makes the desiring thing a friend of what it wants, and need then points toward what is one’s own. The proposal reaches affinity, but the next passage still has to distinguish that affinity from mere likeness.

revisions.title: An interruption leaves the question open
revisions.body: The inquiry ends without converting its last proposals into a definition. Socrates gathers the candidates into a conditional: if none of the examined possibilities is the friend, he has nothing more to say. Then the paidagogoi break up the gathering, so the dialogue closes with its unanswered question still alive.

body: "I read this exchange as a stress test for two attractive formulas. On that reading, “opposite befriends opposite” sounds explanatory until the conversation turns it against friendship with an enemy, then against justice and goodness. The passage need not announce a third category; its sharper achievement is to leave both formulas under pressure. What, then, might friendship require beyond resemblance or opposition?"

The pressure is cumulative: the oikeion proposal revives rejected like-to-like consequences (claim_lysis_0027; claim_lysis_0028; rel_lysis_0001), while identifying good with oikeion yields only the conditional that good is friend to good (claim_lysis_0029; rel_lysis_0001).
